h1: Marketing beer where alcohol advertising is restricted
title: Marketing Beer Where Ads Are Restricted | Craft Beer School
desc: How breweries market beer when alcohol advertising is limited: owned channels, the product itself, events and the rules to check first.
teaser: Some countries limit alcohol ads hard. Brands there still grow, by putting the effort where the rules leave room.
standfirst: Alcohol advertising rules differ widely by country and change over time. This guide shows how brewers build a brand inside tight limits without gambling with a licence.
sections: Start with the rules, not the idea

Before you plan a single post, find out what your market actually restricts. Some countries ban broadcast advertising for alcohol. Others limit where it can appear, what it can show or who it can be aimed at. Many apply rules to social media in the same way as to print.

The rules also differ inside countries. A national law may sit beside regional or city rules. Industry codes often add a second layer on top. Read the regulator's own guidance rather than a blog post, ours included. If the stakes are real, pay for an hour with a local adviser who handles alcohol marketing.

Keep a one-page note of what you found: what is banned, what is allowed with conditions, who checks and how they check. Everything else in the plan hangs off that page.

The details vary, but several themes turn up again and again across countries. Ads must not target minors or appear where minors are likely to be the main audience. Ads must not link drinking with driving, sporting success or social victory. Health claims are usually off the table. Many places require a responsibility message or restrict the people who may appear in an ad to those who are clearly adults.

Treat these as a starting list of questions, not as a statement of the law where you sell. Your regulator may be stricter or looser on every point.
Put the effort into the product and the place

When paid reach is limited, the beer, the label and the room do the selling. A distinctive can design, a taproom people want to be seen in and a clear name travel further than a banner ever will. Look at packaging choices as a marketing decision, because the pack is the one piece of media you fully control.

Where the law allows it, point of sale matters more than usual. A tap handle, a coaster or a shelf strip is often treated differently from advertising, but not everywhere. Ask first.
Owned channels and word of mouth

An email list, a website and a physical venue are yours. They do not depend on an ad platform's policy changing next month. Collect addresses only from adults and only with clear consent, then send news about releases and events.

Check how each platform treats alcohol before you rely on it. Some allow organic posts but refuse paid promotion. Some require age gates. Our guide to Instagram for breweries covers what to post when reach is organic only.

Tasting events, collaborations with local chefs and brewery tours produce stories that people repeat without being paid to. They also give you a chance to meet customers in person and to confirm their age.

Wherever you are, build age checks into every channel you control. A simple date-of-birth gate is the minimum, not the aim. Hold a cautious tone. No post should suggest that more drinking is better. None should read as aimed at young people.

Many brewers also make a no- and low-alcohol beer. Where alcohol is banned outright, that is the only product you may market. Local law comes first. See marketing non-alcoholic beer in the Gulf for how that works.

Sponsorships and influencer posts are the grey area. In some countries an influencer who posts about your beer is treated exactly as if you had run an ad. You are responsible for what they say. Give any partner a written brief that includes the age rules, the banned claims and the responsibility message.

Collaborations with restaurants and food makers are usually safer ground, because the story is about the dish and the producer. Still ask your regulator whether co-branded menus count as advertising. Keep copies of everything you approve, since a regulator will ask for evidence if someone complains.
A plan you can run next week

1. Write the one-page rules note for your market.
  2. List every channel you own: venue, website, email list and social profiles.
  3. Choose two events a year that you can host or join.
  4. Brief your staff on what they may and may not say, because a taproom employee is an advertisement too.
  5. Review the note every six months, since rules move.

This is the gap many small breweries feel. They know their beer but not how to turn a restricted market into a channel plan. A structured course on digital marketing for breweries gives you the planning frame, with room to ask questions about your own market.
faqs: No. Rules differ by country and sometimes by region. Check with your national regulator or a local adviser before you spend on any campaign.
Is social media treated as advertising?
In many places yes. Platforms also add their own alcohol policies on top of the law. Read both.
What can I do if paid ads are banned?
Focus on the product, the venue, events, email and word of mouth, all within local rules.
Often they do in some form, for example age limits and licence conditions. Ask your regulator.
